decks.title: Metals and Non-metals — Part 1: Properties and the reactivity series
goals: Compare metals and non-metals by their physical properties, including the exceptions
Write equations for reactions of metals with oxygen, water, dilute acids and salt solutions
Identify amphoteric oxides and explain why some metals react only with steam
Arrange metals in order of reactivity from displacement evidence

slides.heading: Metals and Non-metals
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how metals and non-metals differ in look and feel, how metals react with oxygen, water, acids and salt solutions, and how we rank them in the **reactivity series**.

visual.alt: Sodium reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas
visual.caption: This reaction is why sodium is never kept in the open.

slides.narration: Namaste! Look around your home: a steel tiffin, copper wires behind the switchboard, an aluminium pressure cooker, a silver anklet. Now think of the oxygen you breathe, the carbon in a pencil and the sulphur in fireworks. Metals and non-metals behave very differently. Some metals are so reactive that they catch fire in water, while gold stays bright for thousands of years. In this part we find out why, and learn to rank metals by reactivity.

slides.heading: Metals and non-metals at a glance
slides.body_md: Most elements are metals. Metals are usually **lustrous, hard, malleable, ductile, sonorous** and good **conductors**. Non-metals usually lack these properties.

visual.alt: Table comparing metals and non-metals for state, lustre, malleability, conductivity and sonority, with the main exceptions

slides.narration: Here is the big picture. Metals are usually shiny, can be beaten and pulled into new shapes, conduct heat and electricity, and ring when you strike them. That ringing is why temple bells and school bells are made of metal. Non-metals are usually dull and brittle, and conduct poorly. Notice the exceptions in brackets: mercury is a liquid metal, bromine is a liquid non-metal, iodine shines and graphite conducts. Examiners love these exceptions.

slides.heading: Malleable and ductile
slides.body_md: **Malleable**: can be beaten into thin sheets. **Ductile**: can be drawn into thin wires. Gold and silver are the most malleable metals; a single gram of gold can be drawn into a wire about 2 km long.

slides.narration: Have you seen the shiny silver layer on kaju katli? That is silver varq, silver beaten so thin that it is lighter than a feather. That is malleability. Now look at the copper wires in an electric cable. Copper is pulled through smaller and smaller holes until it becomes a thin wire. That is ductility. Gold is the champion of both: one gram of gold can be drawn into a wire about two kilometres long.

slides.heading: Good conductors of heat
slides.body_md: Metals conduct **heat** well; **silver** and **copper** are the best. **Lead** and **mercury** are comparatively poor conductors. Cooking vessels have metal bodies but plastic or wooden handles.

slides.narration: Stick a few pins under a copper rod with drops of wax, and heat one end. The wax nearest the flame melts first and that pin drops. Then the next one falls, and the next, as heat flows along the metal. Metals also conduct electricity, which is why wires are made of copper and aluminium, wrapped in plastic. Next time you hold a pressure cooker by its handle, notice that the handle is made of a poor conductor.

slides.heading: Exceptions you must know
slides.body_md: General rules have important exceptions.
columns:
**Metals that break the rules**

- **Sodium** and **potassium** are so soft they can be cut with a knife, and have low melting points.
- **Mercury** is a liquid at room temperature.
- **Gallium** and **caesium** melt on your palm.
- **Lead** and **mercury** conduct heat poorly.

**Non-metals that break the rules**

- **Iodine** is lustrous.
- **Graphite**, a form of carbon, conducts electricity.
- **Diamond**, another form of carbon, is the hardest natural substance and has a very high melting point.
- **Bromine** is a liquid.
slides.narration: Rules in science come with exceptions, and you must know them. Sodium and potassium are metals, yet you can slice them like cold butter. Mercury is a metal, yet it flows. Gallium melts in your hand. On the other side, iodine crystals shine, graphite in your pencil conducts electricity, and diamond, also pure carbon, is the hardest natural substance known. So never classify an element from one property alone.

slides.heading: Quick check: metal or non-metal?
slides.body_md: An element is shiny, brittle and does not conduct electricity. What is it most likely to be?
slides.narration: Quick check. Look at all three properties together, not just the first one. Remember the exceptions from the last slide, and choose the element that fits every clue.

slides.heading: Metals with oxygen: basic oxides
slides.body_md: Metals combine with oxygen to form **metal oxides**, which are generally **basic**. Soluble ones, such as sodium oxide, dissolve in water to give **alkalis**.

visual.alt: Aluminium and oxygen form aluminium oxide
visual.caption: Copper turns black on heating because copper(II) oxide forms on its surface.

slides.narration: Heat a strip of copper and it gets coated with a black layer of copper oxide. Aluminium forms a thin layer of aluminium oxide even at room temperature. Most metal oxides behave as bases: they react with acids to give salt and water. A few, like sodium oxide and potassium oxide, dissolve in water to form alkalis. Remember the pattern from the last chapter: metal oxides are basic, non-metal oxides are acidic.

slides.heading: Amphoteric oxides: both acid and base
slides.body_md: **Amphoteric oxides** react with **both acids and bases** to give salt and water. Examples: **aluminium oxide** and **zinc oxide**.

visual.alt: Aluminium oxide reacts with sodium hydroxide to give sodium aluminate and water

slides.narration: Most oxides choose a side, but a few are happy to play for both teams. Aluminium oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to give aluminium chloride and water, as a base would. It also reacts with sodium hydroxide to give sodium aluminate and water, as an acid would. Oxides like this are called amphoteric, from a Greek word meaning both. Zinc oxide is another example. In exams, give one equation for each side.

slides.heading: How eagerly do metals react with oxygen?
slides.body_md: Different metals react with oxygen at very different rates.

rows: React so vigorously that they catch fire; stored under kerosene
Burns with a dazzling white flame when heated
Form a thin protective oxide layer that stops further reaction
Does not burn as a lump, but iron filings burn with sparks
Does not burn; gets a black coat of copper oxide
Do not react, even on strong heating

visual.alt: Table of how strongly different metals react with oxygen, from potassium and sodium that catch fire to silver and gold that do not react

slides.narration: Metals show a clear ladder of eagerness. Potassium and sodium react so fast that they can catch fire in air, so they are kept under kerosene. Magnesium burns with a brilliant white light. Aluminium and zinc quickly form a thin oxide skin that protects the metal below, which is why an aluminium kadhai does not crumble. Iron filings sparkle in a flame, like a phuljhadi. Copper only blackens, and silver and gold do not react at all.

slides.heading: Metals with water: a ladder of reactivity
slides.body_md: Reactive metals give a **metal hydroxide** (with cold or hot water) or a **metal oxide** (with steam), and **hydrogen**.

visual.alt: Table of how metals react with cold water, hot water and steam, from violent with potassium to no reaction with copper, silver and gold

slides.narration: Water sorts metals into groups. Potassium and sodium react violently with cold water; so much heat is released that the hydrogen catches fire. Calcium reacts gently, and bubbles of hydrogen stick to it so that it floats. Magnesium needs hot water and also floats. Aluminium, zinc and iron ignore water, but react with steam to give an oxide and hydrogen. Lead, copper, silver and gold do not react with water at all.

slides.heading: Metals that react only with steam
slides.body_md: Steam from wet glass wool passes over the **heated metal**; **hydrogen** is collected over water.

slides.narration: To test a metal like iron with steam, push wet glass wool to the closed end of a boiling tube and place the metal a little further along. Heat both: the glass wool makes steam, and the steam passes over the hot metal. The hydrogen formed travels through the delivery tube and collects in an inverted gas jar. Iron gives a black oxide with three iron atoms and four oxygen atoms. Note that the products are oxides, not hydroxides.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sodium in water
slides.body_md: Imran's teacher drops a tiny piece of sodium into a trough of water; it darts around and a flame appears. Write the balanced equation and explain the flame.
bullets: Step 1 — reactants: sodium and water; products: sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.
Step 2 — skeletal equation: $\ce{Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2}$.
Step 3 — hydrogen is 2 on the left and 3 on the right; make NaOH and $\ce{H2O}$ two each, then Na two: $\ce{2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2}$.
Step 4 — check: Na 2 = 2, H 4 = 4, O 2 = 2.
Step 5 — the reaction is highly **exothermic**, so the hydrogen produced catches fire.

visual.alt: Atom check for sodium and water: two sodium, four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms on each side

slides.narration: Let us work it out. Sodium and water give sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. In the skeletal equation hydrogen does not balance: two on the left, three on the right. Put a two before water and a two before sodium hydroxide, then a two before sodium. Now count: two sodium, four hydrogen, two oxygen on each side. The flame appears because the reaction gives out so much heat that the hydrogen ignites. This is a demonstration only for teachers.

slides.heading: Quick check: steam only
slides.body_md: Which metal reacts with steam but not with cold or hot water?
slides.narration: Quick check. Picture the water ladder from two slides ago. Which group needed steam before it would react? Choose the metal from that group.

slides.body_md: Metals above hydrogen in reactivity give **salt + hydrogen** with dilute hydrochloric or sulphuric acid. The rate of bubbling shows how reactive each metal is: **Mg > Al > Zn > Fe**. Copper does not react.

The faster the bubbles, the more reactive the metal. This simple test lets you rank metals in your own school lab.

slides.heading: Why nitric acid is different
slides.body_md: Metals do not usually give **hydrogen** with **nitric acid**. Nitric acid is a strong **oxidising agent**: it oxidises the hydrogen to water and is itself reduced to oxides of nitrogen. Exceptions: **magnesium** and **manganese** give hydrogen with **very dilute** nitric acid.

nodes.label: Nitric acid oxidises it to water
Oxides of nitrogen are given off instead

visual.alt: Flow: hydrogen formed by a metal in nitric acid is oxidised to water, so oxides of nitrogen are released instead of hydrogen

slides.narration: Here is a twist. If you use nitric acid instead of hydrochloric acid, you usually collect no hydrogen. Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent. Any hydrogen that forms is immediately oxidised to water, and the acid itself turns into oxides of nitrogen. The two exceptions to remember are magnesium and manganese, which do give hydrogen, but only with very dilute nitric acid.

slides.heading: Quick check: no bubbles
slides.body_md: Which metal will **not** give hydrogen with dilute hydrochloric acid?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about where each metal sits compared with hydrogen in reactivity. Only metals more reactive than hydrogen can push it out of an acid.

slides.heading: Metals with salt solutions: displacement
slides.body_md: A **more reactive** metal displaces a **less reactive** metal from a solution of its salt. No reaction occurs the other way round.

visual.alt: Zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate solution; the blue solution becomes colourless and reddish-brown copper deposits
visual.caption: Zinc is above copper, so it displaces copper; copper cannot displace zinc.

slides.narration: Displacement is a competition. Put zinc in blue copper sulphate solution and the blue fades as reddish-brown copper coats the zinc. Zinc is more reactive, so it pushes copper out of its compound. Now put copper in zinc sulphate solution: nothing happens, because copper is the weaker of the two. Copper can still displace silver from silver nitrate, because silver is even less reactive. Displacement results are how chemists built the reactivity series.

slides.heading: The reactivity series
slides.body_md: Metals arranged in order of **decreasing reactivity**. Hydrogen is included as a reference point.

slides.narration: Here is the full reactivity series you need for Class Ten. A popular memory aid starts: Please Stop Calling Me A Zebra, I Like Her Call Me Smart Goat, for potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, hydrogen, copper, mercury, silver and gold. Metals near the top react with cold water; the next few need steam. Every metal above hydrogen gives hydrogen with dilute acids, and none below it does.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: ranking metals from displacement
slides.body_md: Kiran dips strips of three metals, P, Q and R, into solutions of each other's sulphates and records whether a coating appears. Rank P, Q and R.
bullets: Step 1 — P displaces Q and R, so P is more reactive than both.
Step 2 — R displaces Q, so R is more reactive than Q.
Step 3 — Q displaces neither, so it is the least reactive.
Step 4 — order: **P > R > Q**.
Check — every "yes" in the table has the more reactive metal as the strip.

visual.alt: Displacement results for metals P, Q and R: P displaces Q and R, R displaces Q, Q displaces neither

slides.narration: Read the table one row at a time. Metal P coats itself in both other solutions, so P beats both Q and R. Metal R beats Q but not P. Metal Q beats nobody. So the order is P, then R, then Q. A quick way to check: count the yeses in each row. Two yeses means most reactive, zero means least. Questions like this appear often as data-based questions.

slides.heading: Quick check: will it displace?
slides.body_md: Which pair will react?
slides.narration: Last check for this part. For each pair, find both metals on the reactivity series. A reaction happens only if the free metal is above the metal in the salt.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Metals: lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous, good conductors; non-metals: mostly the opposite — learn the exceptions.
Metal oxides are basic; $\ce{Al2O3}$ and $\ce{ZnO}$ are amphoteric.
Reactive metals + water → hydroxide + hydrogen; Al, Zn, Fe + steam → oxide + hydrogen.
Metals above hydrogen + dilute HCl → salt + hydrogen; nitric acid usually gives no hydrogen.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution.

rows: metal + water → hydroxide or oxide + hydrogen
more reactive metal displaces less reactive

visual.alt: Summary table of the four kinds of reactions of metals with an example of each

slides.narration: Let us wrap up Part 1. Metals and non-metals differ in lustre, malleability, ductility, sound and conductivity, but each rule has exceptions. Metals form basic oxides, and aluminium and zinc oxides are amphoteric. Metals react with water, acids and salt solutions in an order that gives us the reactivity series. Read the table aloud once, then try writing each example equation from memory.

slides.heading: Exam tips: properties and reactions of metals
bullets: Name the exception when asked: mercury (liquid metal), bromine (liquid non-metal), iodine (lustrous), graphite (conductor), diamond (hardest).
With steam, the product is a metal **oxide**: $\ce{3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$, not $\ce{Fe(OH)2}$.
Amphoteric: always write **two** equations, one with an acid and one with a base.
Displacement: state the reactivity reason, e.g. "zinc is more reactive than copper".
Explain why nitric acid gives no hydrogen: it is an oxidising agent.
A typical 3-mark answer: observation (1) + balanced equation (1) + reason from reactivity (1).
slides.narration: Here is how to collect every mark. When a question mentions an exception, name the element. With steam, remember that iron gives an oxide, not a hydroxide. For amphoteric oxides, write two equations. In displacement answers, always add the reason from reactivity. If nitric acid appears, explain that it oxidises hydrogen to water. And in a three-mark question, examiners look for an observation, a balanced equation and a reason.

slides.heading: Ionic compounds, metallurgy and corrosion
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how metals and non-metals **bond**, how metals are **extracted** from their ores and **refined**, and how we protect them from **corrosion**.

nodes.label: Ionic compounds: metals give electrons to non-metals
Metallurgy: getting metals out of ores

visual.alt: Route map for Part 2: ionic bonding, then extraction of metals, then corrosion and its prevention

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 2. Why does common salt melt only at a very high temperature, yet dissolve so easily in water? How do we get shiny metals out of dull rocks dug from mines in Rajasthan and Jharkhand? And why does an iron gate rust while a stainless steel spoon stays bright? All three answers come from one idea you met in Part 1: how readily metals give away electrons.

slides.heading: Why atoms bond: the stable octet
slides.body_md: **Noble gases** have completely filled outer shells (8 electrons, or 2 for helium) and are very unreactive. Other atoms **lose or gain electrons** to reach such a stable arrangement, forming **ions**.

visual.alt: Table showing sodium and magnesium losing electrons and chlorine and oxygen gaining electrons to reach noble-gas configurations

slides.narration: Neon and argon hardly react with anything, because their outer shells are full. Other atoms try to copy them. Sodium has just one electron in its outer shell, so it is easier to lose that one than to gain seven. Chlorine has seven, so it is easier to gain one. A metal atom that loses electrons becomes a positive ion, called a cation. A non-metal atom that gains electrons becomes a negative ion, called an anion.

slides.heading: Forming sodium chloride
slides.body_md: Sodium **transfers** one electron to chlorine. The oppositely charged ions, $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$, attract each other strongly: an **ionic (electrovalent) bond**.

slides.narration: Magnesium has two electrons to give away, but a chlorine atom needs only one. So one magnesium atom shares out its two electrons to two chlorine atoms. The result is one magnesium ion with a charge of two plus, and two chloride ions each with a charge of one minus. The charges add up to zero, which is why the formula of magnesium chloride has two chlorines. Always check that the charges in an ionic formula cancel out.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: forming calcium oxide
slides.body_md: Show how calcium (atomic number 20) and oxygen (atomic number 8) form calcium oxide.
bullets: Step 1 — configurations: Ca 2, 8, 8, 2; O 2, 6.
Step 2 — calcium loses its 2 outer electrons → $\ce{Ca^2+}$ (2, 8, 8).
Step 3 — oxygen gains those 2 electrons → $\ce{O^2-}$ (2, 8).
Step 4 — charges: (+2) + (−2) = 0, so one of each: formula $\ce{CaO}$.
Check — both ions now have noble-gas configurations (argon and neon).

visual.alt: Worked table: calcium loses two electrons and oxygen gains two, forming calcium and oxide ions with noble-gas configurations

slides.narration: Calcium oxide is quicklime, the substance in whitewash. Calcium has two outer electrons and oxygen needs two, so this time one atom of each is enough. Calcium gives both electrons to oxygen, becoming a calcium ion with charge two plus. Oxygen becomes an oxide ion with charge two minus. Plus two and minus two cancel, so the formula is simply calcium oxide, one to one. Always finish by checking the charges.

slides.heading: Properties of ionic compounds
slides.body_md: Strong forces between oppositely charged ions explain their properties.

rows: Ions are held firmly in a regular arrangement; a sharp blow shatters it
A lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong attraction between ions
Soluble in water, not in kerosene or petrol
Water molecules attract and separate the ions; kerosene does not
Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved
The ions are then free to move and carry charge
The ions are fixed in place

visual.alt: Table of five properties of ionic compounds and the reason for each

slides.narration: Every property of an ionic compound comes from the strong pull between its ions. Because the pull is strong, the solid is hard and melts only at very high temperatures; table salt melts at about eight hundred degrees Celsius. Because water can pull the ions apart, salt dissolves in water but not in kerosene. And because ions carry charge, a salt solution conducts electricity, as long as the ions are free to move.

slides.heading: Why solid salt does not conduct, but molten salt does
slides.body_md: In the solid, ions are **locked** in place. When the compound **melts** or **dissolves**, the ions move towards the oppositely charged electrodes and carry current.

slides.heading: Ores, minerals and gangue
slides.body_md: **Minerals** are natural compounds of elements in the earth's crust. A mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably is an **ore**. Ores are mixed with earthy impurities called **gangue**. Where a metal is found depends on its reactivity.

rows: Often free (native); copper and silver also as sulphides or oxides

visual.alt: Table showing that unreactive metals occur free, middle metals as oxides, sulphides and carbonates, and highly reactive metals only in compounds

slides.narration: Metals hide in rocks in different ways. Gold is so unreactive that it can be found as pure flakes in river sand. Zinc and iron are found combined with oxygen, sulphur or carbonate, in ores such as zinc blende and haematite. Very reactive metals like sodium and aluminium are never found free. The rock dug out also contains sand, soil and other unwanted material, called gangue, which must be removed first.

slides.heading: Steps in getting a metal
slides.body_md: Every extraction follows three broad steps; the **middle step depends on reactivity**.

nodes.label: Low reactivity: heat the ore alone
Middle: roast or calcine to the oxide, then reduce
High reactivity: electrolysis of the molten compound

visual.alt: Flow chart: concentrate the ore, then extract by heating alone, by roasting or calcining and reduction, or by electrolysis depending on reactivity, then refine

slides.narration: Think of extraction as a three-step recipe. First, concentrate the ore by removing gangue, using differences in properties such as density or magnetism. Second, extract the metal, and here the method depends on reactivity: heat alone for metals low in the series, roasting or calcination followed by reduction for metals in the middle, and electrolysis for the most reactive. Third, refine the metal to make it pure.

slides.heading: Low in the series: heat alone is enough
slides.body_md: Oxides of unreactive metals break down on heating. **Mercury** is obtained by heating its sulphide ore, cinnabar, in air; **copper** by heating its sulphide ore in air.

visual.alt: Mercury(II) oxide decomposes on heating to mercury and oxygen

slides.narration: For metals near the bottom of the series, the bond with oxygen is weak. Heat cinnabar, mercury sulphide, in air and it first changes to mercury oxide, which then breaks down on further heating to give liquid mercury. Copper's sulphide ore is partly turned into copper oxide, which then reacts with the remaining sulphide to give copper metal. No extra reducing agent is needed: heat does all the work.

slides.heading: Middle of the series: roasting and calcination
slides.body_md: It is easier to obtain a metal from its **oxide**. So sulphide and carbonate ores are first converted into oxides.

visual.alt: Table comparing roasting of sulphide ores in excess air with calcination of carbonate ores in limited air, with zinc examples

slides.narration: Zinc ores come in two kinds. Zinc blende is a sulphide, so it is roasted: heated strongly in plenty of air, which turns it into zinc oxide and releases sulphur dioxide. Calamine is a carbonate, so it is calcined: heated strongly in limited air, which drives off carbon dioxide and leaves zinc oxide. To remember which is which, roasting needs a roaring supply of air, while calcination works on carbonates.

slides.heading: Reducing the oxide
slides.body_md: The metal oxide is **reduced** with a suitable reducing agent such as **carbon (coke)**, or with a **more reactive metal**.

visual.alt: Zinc oxide is reduced by carbon to zinc metal and carbon monoxide

slides.narration: Once the ore is an oxide, we take the oxygen away. Heating zinc oxide with coke, which is nearly pure carbon, gives zinc metal and carbon monoxide. Carbon is the reducing agent: it is oxidised while zinc oxide is reduced. Sometimes a more reactive metal does the job instead. Aluminium powder reduces manganese dioxide to manganese, and the reaction releases so much heat that the manganese comes out molten.

slides.heading: Thermit welding of railway tracks
slides.body_md: Aluminium reduces iron(III) oxide in a highly **exothermic** reaction. The molten iron produced is used to **join broken rails** and machine parts.

slides.narration: Railway engineers sometimes need to join rails right on the track. They place a crucible above the gap and light a mixture of iron oxide and aluminium powder. Aluminium, being more reactive, snatches the oxygen from iron oxide. So much heat is released that the iron formed is molten, and it flows into the gap and welds the rails together. This is the thermit reaction, and it is a displacement reaction too.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: choosing an extraction method
slides.body_md: For each ore, choose an extraction method from the metal's position in the reactivity series.
bullets: Step 1 — cinnabar, $\ce{HgS}$: mercury is low in the series → heat in air alone.
Step 2 — calamine, $\ce{ZnCO3}$: zinc is in the middle; carbonate → calcine, then reduce with carbon.
Step 3 — rock salt, $\ce{NaCl}$: sodium is high → electrolysis of molten sodium chloride.
Step 4 — haematite, $\ce{Fe2O3}$: iron is in the middle; already an oxide → reduce with carbon.
Check — carbon cannot be used for sodium: sodium holds on to non-metals more strongly than carbon can pull them away.

visual.alt: Worked table matching four ores to extraction methods according to the metal position in the reactivity series

slides.narration: Here is a reasoning routine you can use for any ore. First, find the metal in the reactivity series. Low metals need only heat. Middle metals must become oxides, by roasting a sulphide or calcining a carbonate, and are then reduced with carbon. High metals need electrolysis. Haematite is already an oxide, so it skips straight to reduction. Notice the check: carbon cannot reduce sodium compounds, because sodium is more reactive than carbon.

slides.heading: Top of the series: electrolytic reduction
slides.body_md: Sodium, magnesium, calcium and aluminium are obtained by **electrolysis of their molten compounds**. The metal forms at the **cathode**, the non-metal at the **anode**. Aluminium comes from molten aluminium oxide (alumina).

visual.alt: Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride gives sodium metal and chlorine gas
visual.caption: The salt must be molten: in water, hydrogen would form at the cathode instead.

slides.narration: The most reactive metals hold on to non-metals so tightly that no ordinary reducing agent can pull them apart. Electricity can. Melt sodium chloride and pass a current through it. Sodium ions gain electrons at the cathode and become sodium metal. Chloride ions give up electrons at the anode and become chlorine gas. The salt must be molten, not dissolved, because in water the cathode would give hydrogen instead of sodium.

slides.body_md: **Anode**: thick block of impure copper. **Cathode**: thin strip of pure copper. **Electrolyte**: acidified copper sulphate solution. Pure copper builds up on the cathode; insoluble impurities settle as **anode mud**.

slides.heading: Corrosion: rust and tarnish
slides.body_md: **Corrosion** is the slow eating away of a metal by substances around it. Silver turns **black** (silver sulphide), copper gets a **green** coat (basic copper carbonate), and iron **rusts** — but only when **both air and water** are present.

rows: Tap water, tube open to air
Boiled water covered with an oil layer
Dry air over anhydrous calcium chloride

visual.alt: Table of a rusting experiment: only the nail exposed to both air and water rusts
visual.caption: Boiling removes dissolved air; oil stops air dissolving again; calcium chloride keeps the air dry.

slides.narration: Leave an iron nail in three different tubes for a week. In ordinary water open to air, it rusts. In boiled water sealed under oil, there is water but no air, and it stays shiny. In a dry tube with calcium chloride, there is air but no water, and again no rust. So iron needs both air and water to rust. Silver and copper corrode too: an old silver anklet blackens, and a brass or copper lamp turns green.

slides.heading: Preventing rust
slides.body_md: Keep air and water away, or let a more reactive metal corrode instead: **painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising, chrome plating, anodising** and **alloying**. **Galvanising** coats iron with **zinc**; the iron stays protected even if the coating is scratched.

slides.narration: Iron gates are painted, bicycle chains are oiled and machine parts are greased, all to keep out air and water. Buckets and roofing sheets are galvanised, that is, coated with zinc. Here is the clever part: even if the zinc layer is scratched, the iron does not rust, because zinc is more reactive and corrodes first. Taps are chrome plated, and aluminium window frames are anodised to thicken their protective oxide layer.

slides.heading: Alloys: better than the pure metal
slides.body_md: An **alloy** is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal. Alloying improves properties; alloys usually have **lower electrical conductivity** and **lower melting points** than the pure metals.

rows: 22 parts gold + 2 parts silver or copper

visual.alt: Table of six alloys with their components and uses
visual.caption: An alloy of mercury with another metal is called an amalgam.

slides.narration: Pure iron is soft and rusts easily. Add a little carbon and you get hard, strong steel; add nickel and chromium and you get stainless steel for your steel tiffin. Brass and bronze have been made in India for thousands of years, for lamps, utensils and temple bells. Solder melts easily, so it is used to join wires. And pure gold is too soft for jewellery, so jewellers mix in silver or copper to make twenty-two carat gold.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: Metals lose electrons and non-metals gain them, forming ions held by ionic bonds: $\ce{NaCl}$, $\ce{MgCl2}$.
Ionic compounds: hard, high melting and boiling points, soluble in water, conduct when molten or dissolved.
Extraction depends on reactivity: heat alone, oxide then reduction, or electrolysis; copper is refined electrolytically.
Iron rusts only with both air and water; prevent by painting, oiling, galvanising, chrome plating, anodising, alloying.
Alloys: steel, stainless steel, brass, bronze, solder, 22-carat gold.

rows: Roast or calcine, then reduce with carbon
Zinc from zinc blende or calamine

visual.alt: Summary table of extraction methods for metals of low, middle and high reactivity

slides.narration: Let us wrap up the chapter. Metals give electrons to non-metals, forming ions held by strong ionic bonds, which explains the high melting points and conductivity of salts. The reactivity series decides how each metal is extracted: by heat alone, by reduction of the oxide, or by electrolysis, and copper is refined by electrolysis. Finally, corrosion needs air and water, and we fight it with coatings, galvanising and alloys.

slides.heading: Exam tips: ionic compounds, metallurgy and corrosion
bullets: Electron-dot answers: show only outer electrons, use dots and crosses, put brackets and charges on the ions, and write the final formula.
Conductivity: "conducts when molten or in solution, because the ions are free to move" — say **ions**, not electrons.
Roasting = sulphide + excess air; calcination = carbonate + limited air. Write one balanced equation for each.
Refining diagram labels: anode (impure copper), cathode (pure copper), acidified copper sulphate, anode mud, battery terminals.
Rusting needs **both** air (oxygen) and water; galvanising protects even when scratched because zinc is more reactive.
A typical 5-mark metallurgy answer: method chosen with reason (1) + equations (2) + diagram or steps (1) + refining or use (1).
slides.narration: Here is how to score full marks. In electron-dot structures, show only outer electrons, use dots and crosses, and add brackets and charges. When explaining conductivity, say ions, not electrons. Keep roasting and calcination straight, with an equation for each. Learn every label in the copper refining diagram. For rusting, the words both air and water matter. And for galvanising, explain why a scratch does not let the iron rust.

sections.heading: 1. Physical properties of metals and non-metals
sections.body_md:
**Metals** are generally lustrous, hard, **malleable** (beaten into sheets), **ductile** (drawn into wires), **sonorous** (ring when struck), good **conductors of heat and electricity**, and have high melting points. Gold and silver are the most malleable and ductile; silver and copper are the best conductors.

**Non-metals** are solids or gases (bromine is a liquid), generally dull, brittle and poor conductors.

**Exceptions**
- Mercury is a liquid metal; gallium and caesium melt on the palm.
- Sodium and potassium are soft (cut with a knife) and have low melting points.
- Lead and mercury are poor conductors of heat.
- Iodine is lustrous; graphite conducts electricity; diamond is the hardest natural substance with a very high melting point.

sections.heading: 2. Chemical properties of metals
sections.body_md:
**With oxygen:** metal + oxygen → metal oxide (basic). Potassium and sodium catch fire in air and are stored under kerosene; magnesium burns with a dazzling flame; aluminium, zinc and lead form a protective oxide layer; iron filings burn; copper forms black CuO; silver and gold do not react.

**Amphoteric oxides** ($\ce{Al2O3}$, $\ce{ZnO}$) react with both acids and bases to give salt and water. Soluble metal oxides (e.g. $\ce{Na2O}$, $\ce{K2O}$) give alkalis.

**With water:** K, Na (violent, hydrogen catches fire) and Ca (steady, floats) react with cold water to give hydroxide + hydrogen; Mg reacts with hot water (floats); Al, Zn, Fe react only with steam to give oxide + hydrogen; Pb, Cu, Ag, Au do not react.

**With dilute acids:** metals above hydrogen give salt + hydrogen; vigour Mg > Al > Zn > Fe; copper does not react. Nitric acid is an oxidising agent and usually gives no hydrogen (except Mg and Mn with very dilute nitric acid).

**With salt solutions:** a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one.

key_terms.definition_md: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases to give salt and water, e.g. $\ce{Al2O3}$, $\ce{ZnO}$.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its salt solution.

sections.heading: 3. The reactivity series
sections.body_md:
The **reactivity series** lists metals in order of decreasing reactivity, worked out from their reactions with water, acids and salt solutions:

K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > **[H]** > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au

- Metals above hydrogen displace hydrogen from dilute acids; those below do not.
- A metal displaces any metal below it from a solution of its salt.
- The higher the metal, the harder it is to extract from its compounds.

sections.heading: 4. Formation and properties of ionic compounds
sections.body_md:
Atoms react to reach a stable **noble-gas configuration** (an octet, or a duplet for helium). Metals **lose** electrons to form **cations**; non-metals **gain** electrons to form **anions**. The electrostatic attraction between them is an **ionic (electrovalent) bond**.

- Na (2, 8, 1) → $\ce{Na+}$ (2, 8); Cl (2, 8, 7) → $\ce{Cl-}$ (2, 8, 8): $\ce{NaCl}$.
- Mg (2, 8, 2) gives one electron to each of two Cl atoms: $\ce{MgCl2}$.

**Properties of ionic compounds:** hard, brittle solids; high melting and boiling points (strong attraction between ions); generally soluble in water, insoluble in kerosene and petrol; conduct electricity when molten or in solution (ions free to move) but not in the solid state.

key_terms.definition_md: The attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by transfer of electrons.
A positively charged ion, e.g. $\ce{Na+}$.
A negatively charged ion, e.g. $\ce{Cl-}$.
Eight electrons in the outermost shell, a stable arrangement.

sections.heading: 5. Basic metallurgy
sections.body_md:
**Minerals** are naturally occurring compounds; **ores** are minerals from which metals are extracted profitably; **gangue** is the earthy impurity.

**Steps:** (1) **concentration (enrichment)** of the ore; (2) **extraction** by a method that depends on reactivity; (3) **refining**.

- **Low reactivity** (Hg, Cu): heating the ore alone. Cinnabar gives mercury; copper sulphide gives copper.
- **Middle** (Zn, Fe, Pb): sulphide ores are **roasted** (strong heating in excess air); carbonate ores are **calcined** (strong heating in limited air); the oxide is **reduced** with carbon, or with a more reactive metal such as aluminium (**thermit reaction**, used to weld rails).
- **High** (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al): **electrolytic reduction** of the molten chloride or oxide; the metal forms at the cathode.

**Electrolytic refining of copper:** anode — impure copper; cathode — thin strip of pure copper; electrolyte — acidified copper sulphate solution. Pure copper deposits on the cathode; soluble impurities stay in solution; insoluble ones collect below the anode as **anode mud**.

key_terms.definition_md: A mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably.
Earthy impurities such as sand and soil present in an ore.
Heating a sulphide ore strongly in excess air to convert it into an oxide.
Heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air to convert it into an oxide.
Insoluble impurities that settle below the anode during electrolytic refining.

sections.heading: 6. Corrosion and its prevention; alloys
sections.body_md:
**Corrosion:** silver turns black (silver sulphide), copper gets a green coat (basic copper carbonate), iron rusts. Iron rusts only when **both air (oxygen) and water** are present.

**Prevention:** painting, oiling, greasing, **galvanising** (coating with zinc; protects even when scratched because zinc is more reactive), chrome plating, anodising, alloying.

**Alloys** are homogeneous mixtures of a metal with other metals or a non-metal. Their electrical conductivity and melting point are lower than those of the pure metals.
- Steel: iron + carbon; stainless steel: iron + nickel + chromium.
- Brass: copper + zinc; bronze: copper + tin; solder: lead + tin (low melting point, joins wires).
- Pure gold is 24 carat and soft; 22-carat gold has 22 parts gold and 2 parts silver or copper.
- An alloy of mercury is an **amalgam**.

key_terms.definition_md: Slow eating away of a metal by air, moisture or chemicals around it.
Coating iron or steel with a thin layer of zinc to prevent rusting.
A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal.
An alloy in which one of the metals is mercury.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing a hydroxide as the product of a metal with steam: iron gives $\ce{Fe3O4}$, aluminium gives $\ce{Al2O3}$.
- Forgetting that nitric acid usually gives no hydrogen.
- Electron-dot structures without brackets and charges, or with the electrons drawn on the wrong atom.
- Saying solid ionic compounds conduct, or that electrons carry the current in a salt solution.
- Mixing up roasting (sulphide, excess air) and calcination (carbonate, limited air).
- In refining, swapping the anode (impure copper) and the cathode (pure copper).
- Saying iron rusts in "air" or in "water": it needs both.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, term or value only.
- 2–3-mark answers: balanced equation (1), observation or reason from reactivity (1), name or condition (1).
- 5-mark answers: labelled diagram (1–2), equations (1–2), explanation of steps or properties (1–2).
- Case-based questions: two 1-mark parts from the passage and a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

cards.front_md: What does "malleable" mean? Give an example.
cards.back_md: Can be beaten into thin sheets: silver varq, aluminium foil.

cards.front_md: What does "ductile" mean?
cards.back_md: Can be drawn into thin wires, e.g. copper wire.

cards.front_md: Which metal is liquid at room temperature? Which non-metal?
cards.back_md: Mercury (metal); bromine (non-metal).

cards.front_md: Name a non-metal that conducts electricity and one that is lustrous.
cards.back_md: Graphite conducts; iodine is lustrous.

cards.front_md: Which metals can be cut with a knife?
cards.back_md: Sodium and potassium.

cards.front_md: Are metal oxides acidic or basic?
cards.back_md: Generally **basic**; soluble ones such as $\ce{Na2O}$ give alkalis.

cards.front_md: What is an amphoteric oxide? Give two examples.
cards.back_md: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases: $\ce{Al2O3}$, $\ce{ZnO}$.

cards.front_md: Aluminium oxide + sodium hydroxide gives…?
cards.back_md: $\ce{Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O}$ (sodium aluminate).

cards.front_md: Why are sodium and potassium stored under kerosene?
cards.back_md: They react so vigorously with air and water that they can catch fire.

cards.front_md: Why does calcium float when it reacts with water?
cards.back_md: Bubbles of hydrogen stick to its surface.

cards.front_md: Iron + steam gives…?
cards.back_md: $\ce{3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$ (an oxide, not a hydroxide).

cards.front_md: Why is hydrogen usually not evolved when metals react with nitric acid?
cards.back_md: Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent: it oxidises hydrogen to water.

cards.front_md: Order of reaction rate with dilute HCl: Mg, Fe, Zn, Al?
cards.back_md: Mg > Al > Zn > Fe (copper does not react).

cards.front_md: Reactivity series (Class 10 list)?
cards.back_md: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au

cards.front_md: When does a metal displace another from its salt solution?
cards.back_md: When it is **more reactive** (higher in the series).

cards.front_md: What is an ionic bond?
cards.back_md: The attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by transfer of electrons.

cards.front_md: Electron-dot formation of NaCl in words?
cards.back_md: Na (2, 8, 1) gives its 1 outer electron to Cl (2, 8, 7): $\ce{Na+}$ (2, 8) and $\ce{Cl-}$ (2, 8, 8).

cards.front_md: Why is the formula of magnesium chloride MgCl₂?
cards.back_md: Mg loses 2 electrons; each Cl gains only 1, so two Cl are needed to balance the charge.

cards.front_md: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
cards.back_md: Strong forces of attraction between ions need a lot of energy to overcome.

cards.front_md: When do ionic compounds conduct electricity?
cards.back_md: Only when **molten** or **dissolved**, because the ions are then free to move.

cards.front_md: Define ore and gangue.
cards.back_md: Ore: mineral from which a metal is extracted profitably. Gangue: earthy impurities in the ore.

cards.front_md: Roasting vs calcination?
cards.back_md: Roasting: sulphide ore + excess air. Calcination: carbonate ore + limited air. Both give the oxide.

cards.front_md: Thermit reaction?
cards.back_md: $\ce{Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3 + heat}$: used to weld railway tracks.

cards.front_md: Why are sodium and aluminium extracted by electrolysis, not by carbon?
cards.back_md: They are more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove oxygen or chlorine from their compounds.

cards.front_md: Electrolytic refining of copper: anode, cathode, electrolyte?
cards.back_md: Anode: impure copper; cathode: pure copper strip; electrolyte: acidified copper sulphate.

cards.front_md: What is anode mud?
cards.back_md: Insoluble impurities that settle below the anode during electrolytic refining.

cards.front_md: Conditions needed for iron to rust?
cards.back_md: Both **air (oxygen)** and **water**.

cards.front_md: Why does silver turn black and copper turn green in air?
cards.back_md: Silver forms black silver sulphide; copper forms green basic copper carbonate.

cards.front_md: Why does galvanised iron not rust even when scratched?
cards.back_md: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so zinc corrodes first and protects the iron.

cards.front_md: Composition of brass, bronze and solder?
cards.back_md: Brass: Cu + Zn; bronze: Cu + Sn; solder: Pb + Sn.

cards.front_md: Why is 22-carat gold used for jewellery, not 24-carat?
cards.back_md: Pure (24-carat) gold is too soft; adding silver or copper makes it harder.

cards.front_md: What is an amalgam?
cards.back_md: An alloy in which one of the metals is mercury.

questions.stem_md: Which metal is a **liquid** at room temperature?
questions.solution_md: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature — option (c). Gallium melts just above room temperature (on the palm of the hand), and sodium and lead are solids.

questions.stem_md: A sweet-shop owner in Varanasi decorates kaju katli with silver beaten into a layer thinner than paper. Which property of silver does this use?
questions.solution_md: Beating a metal into thin sheets uses **malleability** — option (a). Ductility is drawing into wires, sonority is ringing when struck, and conductivity is carrying heat or electricity.

questions.stem_md: An element is **shiny**, **brittle** and does **not conduct** electricity. It is most likely:
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Brittleness and non-conduction point to a non-metal; shininess is unusual for a non-metal.
Step 2: Iodine is a lustrous non-metal that is brittle and a non-conductor — option (d).
Step 3: Copper and sodium are metals and conduct; graphite conducts electricity.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d): iodine is a lustrous non-metal

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Graphite is used to make electrodes.

**Reason (R):** Graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Graphite is an exception among non-metals: it conducts electricity, which is exactly why it is used for electrodes (for example in dry cells). R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? All metals are hard.
questions.solution_md: False. Sodium and potassium are so soft that they can be cut with a knife.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Malleability. (b) Good electrical conductivity (also ductility). (c) Sonority. (d) Lustre.

questions.solution_md: Match each use with the property it depends on: thin sheets → malleable; carrying current → conductor (and drawn into wire → ductile); ringing → sonorous; shine → lustrous.

questions.stem_md: Which metal reacts with **steam** but not with cold or hot water?
questions.solution_md: Iron (like aluminium and zinc) reacts only with steam: $\ce{3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$ — option (c). Sodium and calcium react with cold water; copper does not react with water at all.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an **amphoteric** oxide?
questions.solution_md: Zinc oxide reacts with both acids and bases to give salt and water, so it is amphoteric — option (b). Sodium oxide and magnesium oxide are basic; sulphur dioxide is acidic.

questions.stem_md: A metal X burns in air with a dazzling white flame. The white powder formed dissolves slightly in water, and the solution turns red litmus blue. X is most likely:
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A dazzling white flame is characteristic of burning magnesium.
Step 2: Its oxide gives a basic solution: $\ce{MgO + H2O -> Mg(OH)2}$, which turns red litmus blue. So (a).
Step 3: Copper does not burn (it only blackens); sulphur is a non-metal with an acidic oxide; gold does not react with oxygen.

questions.stem_md: Which metal will **not** give hydrogen gas with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.solution_md: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Copper is below hydrogen, so it does not react — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Rahul adds zinc granules to dilute nitric acid but cannot collect any hydrogen. The best explanation is:

options.text_md: zinc is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
nitric acid is a weak acid
nitric acid is an oxidising agent that oxidises the hydrogen to water
zinc forms a protective layer that stops all reactions

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Zinc is above hydrogen and does give hydrogen with dilute hydrochloric acid, so (a) is wrong.
Step 2: Nitric acid is a strong acid, so (b) is wrong, and zinc does react, so (d) is wrong.
Step 3: Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent: it oxidises the hydrogen formed to water and is itself reduced to oxides of nitrogen — option (c).

questions.stem_md: What are the products when iron reacts with steam?
questions.solution_md: $\ce{3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$. Metals that react only with steam give a metal **oxide** and hydrogen, not a hydroxide; no oxygen is released — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of these pairs will react?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A reaction occurs only if the free metal is more reactive than the metal in the salt.
Step 2: Zinc is above lead, so zinc displaces lead: $\ce{Zn + Pb(NO3)2 -> Zn(NO3)2 + Pb}$ — option (d).
Step 3: Copper is below zinc, silver is below copper, and lead is below zinc, so (a), (b) and (c) show no reaction.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sodium is stored under water to keep it away from air.

**Reason (R):** Sodium reacts vigorously with the oxygen of the air.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: sodium reacts violently with water, so it is stored under **kerosene**, not water. R is true: sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen, which is why it must be kept away from air. So option (d).

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d): A false, R true

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A piece of calcium floats on water while it reacts with it.

**Reason (R):** Calcium metal is less dense than water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: calcium floats during the reaction. R is false: calcium is denser than water (it sinks when no reaction occurs). It floats because bubbles of hydrogen stick to its surface. So option (c).

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c): A true, R false

questions.stem_md: True or false? Aluminium reacts with cold water to give hydrogen.
questions.solution_md: False. Aluminium does not react with cold or hot water (its oxide layer also protects it); it reacts only with steam to give aluminium oxide and hydrogen.

questions.stem_md: Oxides that react with both acids and bases to give salt and water are called ___ oxides.
questions.solution_md: **Amphoteric** oxides, e.g. aluminium oxide and zinc oxide.

questions.stem_md: Match each metal in Column A with how it behaves with water in Column B.

match_right.text_md: Does not react with water in any form

questions.solution_md: Sodium reacts violently with cold water (r); magnesium needs hot water (s); iron reacts only with steam (p); copper does not react (q).

questions.stem_md: Aluminium reacts with steam: $\ce{2Al} + \ce{3H2O} \rightarrow \ce{Al2O3} + x\,\ce{H2}$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Hydrogen atoms on the left: $3 \times 2 = 6$.
Step 2: On the right they are all in $\ce{H2}$, so $x = 6 \div 2 = 3$. Oxygen: 3 = 3; aluminium: 2 = 2. So $x$ = 3.

questions.stem_md: Zinc oxide is amphoteric. Write balanced equations to show its reaction with (a) dilute hydrochloric acid and (b) sodium hydroxide solution.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{ZnO + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2O}$

(b) $\ce{ZnO + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2O}$ (sodium zincate)

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: With an acid, zinc oxide behaves as a base: salt (zinc chloride) + water. Check: Zn 1, O 1, H 2, Cl 2.
Step 2: With a base, it behaves as an acid: sodium zincate + water. Check: Zn 1, O 3, Na 2, H 2.

questions.stem_md:
Ajay heats a magnesium ribbon in a flame. It burns, leaving a white powder, which he shakes with a little water.

(a) What would he observe if he dipped red and blue litmus paper into the mixture?
(b) Write balanced equations for both reactions.
(c) What does this show about the nature of metal oxides?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Red litmus turns **blue**; blue litmus stays blue.

(b) $\ce{2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO}$; $\ce{MgO + H2O -> Mg(OH)2}$

(c) Metal oxides are **basic**; those that dissolve in water form alkalis.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Magnesium oxide dissolves slightly to form magnesium hydroxide, a base.
Step 2: Bases turn red litmus blue.
Step 3: Generalise: metal oxides are basic.

questions.stem_md:
Nisha places a crumpled piece of aluminium foil in blue copper(II) chloride solution. For the first few minutes nothing seems to happen; then the solution slowly loses its colour and a reddish-brown deposit appears.

(a) Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
(b) Explain the colour change.
(c) Suggest why the reaction was slow to start.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{2Al + 3CuCl2 -> 2AlCl3 + 3Cu}$

(b) Aluminium is more reactive than copper and displaces it. Blue copper chloride is replaced by colourless aluminium chloride, and copper metal deposits as a reddish-brown solid.

(c) Aluminium is covered by a thin protective layer of aluminium oxide, which must break down before the metal underneath can react.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Balance: aluminium chloride is $\ce{AlCl3}$ and copper chloride is $\ce{CuCl2}$; chlorine needs 6 on each side, so 2 Al, 3 CuCl₂, 2 AlCl₃, 3 Cu.
Step 2: Displacement explained by reactivity; colour from the ions in solution.
Step 3: The delay is due to the oxide layer, not low reactivity.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe how potassium, calcium and magnesium react with water, giving the conditions and a balanced equation for each.
(b) With a labelled diagram, describe how you would show that iron reacts with steam, and write the equation.
(c) Name two metals that do not react with water at all.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Potassium reacts violently with **cold** water; so much heat is given out that the hydrogen catches fire: $\ce{2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2}$.
Calcium reacts less violently with **cold** water; it floats because hydrogen bubbles stick to it: $\ce{Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2}$.
Magnesium reacts with **hot** water and also floats: $\ce{Mg + 2H2O -> Mg(OH)2 + H2}$.

(b) Place wet glass wool at the closed end of a boiling tube and iron filings further along. Clamp the tube nearly horizontal, fit a cork with a delivery tube leading under water into an inverted gas jar, and heat the iron and the glass wool. Steam passes over the hot iron; hydrogen collects in the jar. Labels: boiling tube, wet glass wool, iron, burners, delivery tube, trough of water, gas jar with hydrogen.
$\ce{3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$

(c) Any two of lead, copper, silver, gold.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Order the metals by reactivity with water: K (cold, violent) > Ca (cold, steady) > Mg (hot water).
Step 2: Metals that need steam give an oxide; set up the apparatus so steam meets the hot metal.
Step 3: Metals below iron in the list given in Class 10 do not react with water.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Balanced equation for iron and steam

questions.stem_md: Which list shows metals in **decreasing** order of reactivity?
questions.solution_md: From the reactivity series, Na > Mg > Zn > Cu, so (b). Option (a) is the same list in increasing order.

questions.stem_md: Strips of metals W, X and Y are placed in solutions of each other's salts. W displaces X but not Y; Y displaces both W and X. The order of reactivity is:
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Y displaces both others, so Y is the most reactive.
Step 2: W displaces X, so W > X.
Step 3: Order: Y > W > X — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Of the metals in the reactivity series studied in Class 10, the most reactive is ___ and the least reactive is ___.
questions.solution_md: The series starts with **potassium** and ends with **gold**.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A copper wire placed in colourless silver nitrate solution will become coated with silver.
questions.solution_md: True. Copper is above silver in the reactivity series, so it displaces silver: $\ce{Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag}$. The solution also turns blue.

questions.stem_md:
Pooja tests four metals, A, B, C and D, and records:

| Metal | Dilute HCl | In copper sulphate solution | In iron(II) sulphate solution |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | bubbles slowly | coated with copper | no change |
| B | no bubbles | no change | no change |
| C | bubbles fast | coated with copper | coated with iron |
| D | bubbles steadily | coated with copper | coated with iron |

(a) Arrange A, B, C and D in decreasing order of reactivity.
(b) Which metal could be copper? Give a reason.
(c) Which metal could be iron? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) C > D > A > B.

(b) **B**: it does not react with dilute acid, so it is below hydrogen, and it does not displace copper or iron.

(c) **A**: it reacts slowly with acid and displaces copper but not iron — exactly what iron itself would do (a metal cannot displace itself from iron(II) sulphate).

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Metals that displace iron (C, D) are above iron; the faster bubbling of C puts C above D.
Step 2: A displaces copper but not iron, so it lies between iron and copper or is iron itself; it reacts with acid, so it is above hydrogen.
Step 3: B reacts with nothing: least reactive, consistent with copper.

questions.stem_md:
A jeweller in Jaipur receives an unknown grey metal, M. He wants to find where it fits in the reactivity series using only strips of zinc, iron and copper, solutions of zinc sulphate, iron(II) sulphate, copper sulphate and M sulphate, and dilute hydrochloric acid.

(a) Plan a set of tests and explain how each result would place M.
(b) In his tests, M displaces copper from copper sulphate but not iron from iron(II) sulphate, and iron displaces M from M sulphate. Where does M fit? Write a general equation for one reaction.
(c) Would M give hydrogen with dilute hydrochloric acid? Explain whether his results alone can answer this.
(d) Evaluate one limitation of judging reactivity by speed of bubbling with acid.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Put a strip of M into zinc sulphate, iron(II) sulphate and copper sulphate solutions, and put strips of zinc, iron and copper into M sulphate. A coating on M in a solution means M is above that metal; a coating on another metal in M sulphate means that metal is above M. Also add M to dilute hydrochloric acid and watch for bubbles.

(b) M is **below iron and above copper**. For example: $\ce{M + CuSO4 -> MSO4 + Cu}$ (for a metal forming $\ce{M^2+}$ ions).

(c) The displacement results alone cannot decide, because hydrogen lies between iron and copper too. The acid test is needed: if M bubbles with dilute hydrochloric acid, it is above hydrogen (like lead); if not, it is below hydrogen.

(d) The speed of bubbling depends also on the surface area and cleanliness of the metal (an oxide layer, as on aluminium, can slow it down) and on the concentration and temperature of the acid, so the test must be done under identical conditions; displacement gives a clearer yes/no answer.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Design paired displacement tests in both directions.
Step 2: Interpret: M > Cu, Fe > M, so Fe > M > Cu.
Step 3: Recognise that hydrogen's place in that gap needs a separate acid test.
Step 4: Evaluate the bubbling method by naming variables that affect rate besides reactivity.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Sensible plan with interpretation of results
(b) Correct position (Fe > M > Cu) with an equation
(d) One valid limitation (surface area / oxide layer / conditions)

questions.stem_md: When magnesium forms magnesium chloride, each magnesium atom:
questions.solution_md: Magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses its two outer electrons, one to each of two chlorine atoms, and becomes $\ce{Mg^2+}$ (2, 8) — option (c). Metals lose electrons; ionic compounds form by transfer, not sharing.

questions.stem_md: The electronic configuration of the chloride ion, $\ce{Cl-}$, is:
questions.solution_md: Chlorine (atomic number 17) is 2, 8, 7. Gaining one electron gives 2, 8, 8 — option (b), the configuration of argon.

questions.stem_md: A white solid S does not conduct electricity, but conducts well when melted. It dissolves in water but not in petrol. S is most likely:
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Conducting only when molten, and dissolving in water but not in petrol, are properties of an ionic compound.
Step 2: Potassium bromide is ionic — option (a).
Step 3: Sugar, wax and naphthalene are covalent: they do not conduct even when melted, and wax and naphthalene dissolve in petrol rather than water.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but its aqueous solution does.

**Reason (R):** In the solid state, the ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Conduction needs moving charges; in the solid the ions are fixed, while in solution they are free to move. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Ionic compounds generally dissolve readily in kerosene and petrol.
questions.solution_md: False. Ionic compounds are generally soluble in water but insoluble in solvents such as kerosene and petrol.

questions.stem_md: Positively charged ions are called ___ and negatively charged ions are called ___.
questions.solution_md: **Cations** (e.g. $\ce{Na+}$) and **anions** (e.g. $\ce{Cl-}$).

questions.stem_md: How many electrons in total are present in one magnesium ion, $\ce{Mg^2+}$? (Atomic number of Mg = 12.)
questions.solution_md: A magnesium atom has 12 electrons (2, 8, 2). It loses 2 to form $\ce{Mg^2+}$, so it has $12 - 2 = 10$ electrons (2, 8).

questions.stem_md: Show, using electron-dot structures, the formation of potassium chloride from its atoms. (Atomic numbers: K = 19, Cl = 17.)

answer.model_answer_md:
K (2, 8, 8, 1) has one outer electron; Cl (2, 8, 7) has seven.

K× + ·Cl (seven outer electrons shown as dots) → [K]⁺ [×Cl, eight outer electrons]⁻

Potassium transfers its outer electron to chlorine, forming $\ce{K+}$ (2, 8, 8) and $\ce{Cl-}$ (2, 8, 8), which are held by an ionic bond: $\ce{KCl}$.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Write configurations and outer electrons.
Step 2: Show one electron moving from K to Cl (cross to dots).
Step 3: Write both ions in brackets with charges, and the formula.

marking_scheme.step: Correct electron-dot structures of the atoms with electron transfer shown
Ions with brackets and charges, and formula KCl

questions.stem_md:
Three solids were tested:

| Solid | Melting point (K) | Conducts as a solid? | Conducts when molten? | Soluble in water? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | 1074 | No | Yes | Yes |
| Q | 353 | No | No | No |
| R | 1358 | Yes | Yes | No |

(a) Which solid is an ionic compound? Give two reasons from the table.
(b) Which solid is a metal? Give one reason.
(c) Explain why P conducts only after it melts.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **P**: it has a high melting point, and it conducts when molten but not as a solid (it also dissolves in water).

(b) **R**: it conducts electricity even as a solid (and has a high melting point).

(c) In solid P the ions are held in fixed positions; when it melts, the ions become free to move and carry the current.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Match the pattern "conducts only when molten or dissolved + high melting point" to ionic compounds.
Step 2: Conducting as a solid is a property of metals (and graphite).
Step 3: Explain with mobility of ions.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Ions fixed in solid, free to move when molten

questions.stem_md:
(a) Using electron-dot structures, show the formation of magnesium chloride from magnesium (atomic number 12) and chlorine (atomic number 17).
(b) Name the type of bond formed and the ions present.
(c) Give three properties of compounds like magnesium chloride, with a reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Mg (2, 8, 2) has two outer electrons; each Cl (2, 8, 7) has seven. One electron goes from Mg to each of two Cl atoms:
Cl (7 dots) + ×Mg× + Cl (7 dots) → [Cl, 8 electrons]⁻ [Mg]²⁺ [Cl, 8 electrons]⁻, i.e. $\ce{MgCl2}$.

(b) **Ionic (electrovalent) bond**; ions $\ce{Mg^2+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$.

(c) Any three:
- Hard, brittle solids — strong attraction between ions in a regular arrangement.
- High melting and boiling points — much energy is needed to overcome the strong attraction.
- Soluble in water, insoluble in kerosene — water separates the ions.
- Conduct electricity when molten or in solution but not as solids — ions are free to move only then.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Show the transfer of two electrons, one to each chlorine.
Step 2: Write brackets and charges; check the charges cancel: (+2) + 2 × (−1) = 0.
Step 3: Link each property to the strong forces between ions or to ion mobility.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Correct electron-dot diagram with transfer to two Cl atoms
(c) Three properties with reasons (2 marks: 1 for properties, 1 for reasons)

questions.stem_md: The earthy impurities such as sand and soil present in an ore are called:
questions.solution_md: Unwanted earthy material mixed with an ore is **gangue** — option (d). A mineral is any naturally occurring compound; alloys and amalgams are metal mixtures.

questions.stem_md: Roasting is:

options.text_md: heating a sulphide ore strongly in excess air
heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air
heating a metal oxide with carbon
passing electricity through a molten ore

questions.solution_md: Roasting converts a sulphide ore into an oxide by strong heating in excess air — option (a). (b) is calcination, (c) is reduction, and (d) is electrolytic reduction.

questions.stem_md: A factory wants to produce **sodium metal**. Which method will work?

options.text_md: Electrolysis of sodium chloride solution in water
Heating sodium chloride strongly in air

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sodium is near the top of the reactivity series, so carbon cannot reduce its compounds, ruling out (a); heating in air does not decompose sodium chloride, ruling out (d).
Step 2: In aqueous solution, hydrogen forms at the cathode instead of sodium (the chlor-alkali process), so (b) fails.
Step 3: Electrolysis of **molten** sodium chloride gives sodium at the cathode — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the thermit process for joining railway tracks, aluminium powder is mixed with iron(III) oxide. Why aluminium?

options.text_md: Aluminium is less reactive than iron, so it is not affected by the heat.
Aluminium oxide is a liquid that fills the gap.
Iron is more reactive than aluminium and pulls oxygen from it.
Aluminium is more reactive than iron, so it removes oxygen from iron oxide, releasing a lot of heat.

questions.solution_md: $\ce{Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3 + heat}$. Aluminium is above iron, so it reduces iron oxide; the reaction is so exothermic that the iron is produced molten and fills the gap — option (d). Options (a) and (c) reverse the reactivity order, and (b) is not the reason.

questions.stem_md: In the electrolytic refining of copper, pure copper is deposited:

options.text_md: on the anode, the thick block of impure copper
on the cathode, a thin strip of pure copper
at the bottom of the tank as anode mud
in the solution as copper sulphate

questions.solution_md: Copper dissolves from the impure anode and an equal amount of pure copper deposits on the cathode — option (b). Anode mud contains the insoluble impurities, not pure copper.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Carbon cannot be used to reduce aluminium oxide to aluminium.

**Reason (R):** Aluminium has a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon has.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Because aluminium holds oxygen more strongly than carbon does, carbon cannot take the oxygen away; aluminium is therefore extracted by electrolysis. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Mercury can be obtained from its ore, cinnabar, by heating alone.

**Reason (R):** Mercury is near the top of the reactivity series.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: $\ce{2HgS + 3O2 -> 2HgO + 2SO2}$, then $\ce{2HgO -> 2Hg + O2}$ on heating. R is false: mercury is near the **bottom** of the series, which is exactly why heat alone works. So option (c).

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c): A true, R false

questions.stem_md: During the electrolytic refining of a metal, the insoluble impurities that collect below the anode are called ___.
questions.solution_md: They form the **anode mud**, which may contain valuable metals such as silver and gold.

questions.stem_md: Match each ore in Column A with the first step used to extract its metal in Column B.

match_right.text_md: Heating in air; the metal is then released by further heating alone

questions.solution_md: 1 — mercury is low in the series: heat alone (r). 2 — a carbonate: calcination (p). 3 — a sulphide: roasting (s). 4 — aluminium is highly reactive: electrolysis (q).

questions.stem_md: In the thermit reaction $\ce{Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3}$, what mass of iron (in g) can be obtained from 320 g of iron(III) oxide? (Fe = 56 u, O = 16 u.)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Molar mass of $\ce{Fe2O3}$ = $2 \times 56 + 3 \times 16 = 160$ g/mol.
Step 2: Moles of $\ce{Fe2O3}$ = $320 \div 160 = 2$ mol.
Step 3: 1 mol $\ce{Fe2O3}$ gives 2 mol Fe, so 2 mol gives 4 mol Fe.
Step 4: Mass of iron = $4 \times 56 = 224$ g.

marking_scheme.step: Molar mass 160 g/mol and moles of oxide = 2
Mole ratio and mass of iron = 224 g

questions.stem_md:
Galena ($\ce{PbS}$) and siderite ($\ce{FeCO3}$) are both converted into oxides before the metal is extracted.

(a) Name the process used for each ore.
(b) Write a balanced equation for each process.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Galena, a sulphide: **roasting** (strong heating in excess air). Siderite, a carbonate: **calcination** (strong heating in limited air).

(b) $\ce{2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2}$; $\ce{FeCO3 -> FeO + CO2}$

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sulphide → roasting; carbonate → calcination.

questions.stem_md:
